standard: CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.6.G.A.1 (area of right triangles and other triangles by composing them into rectangles; other polygons are later missions)
source: Original content written for Pip, aligned to CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.6.G.A.1. No textbook or published lesson was used.
attribution: None required (original content). The standard is cited by its code only.
in_scope: area of a triangle when the base and height are given
putting two copies of a triangle together to make a rectangle or parallelogram
area of a rectangle as base × height (the root skill)
comparing the areas of two triangles
the height goes straight up from the base, not along a slanted side (only if the student brings it up)
out_of_scope: area of a parallelogram as its own formula (next mission)
finding a missing base or height from the area

look_fors: Says two identical copies of the triangle fit together into a rectangle or parallelogram (one sentence is enough)
The shape they make has the same base and height as the triangle (may be implied)
probe_ladder: Why is that wrong? It has a base and a height. I multiplied them.
If I draw my 6 by 4 triangle inside a 6 by 4 box, does it fill the whole box?
What is in the empty part of the box? Is it the same shape as my triangle?
Then a long skinny triangle and a 6 by 4 box with the same base and height take up the same space. That's what my rule says.
concepts.friend_nudge: My cousin said she cut a paper sandwich corner to corner and both pieces matched…? I don't know what that has to do with triangles.

look_fors: Multiplies base by height for the rectangle on one example (6 × 4 = 24)
Walks the example, or corrects Pip's wrong prediction (like adding 6 + 4)
probe_ladder: How big is the shape they make together?
Walk me through a 6 by 4 rectangle. How do you get its area?
I'll guess: a 6 by 4 rectangle is 6 + 4 = 10 squares. Is that right? Count them for me.
Then a 6 by 4 rectangle and a 6 by 4 triangle are both 24. That's what my rule says.
concepts.friend_nudge: Someone in my class said she counts the squares row by row instead of one at a time…? That seems faster.

look_fors: Says one triangle is half of the rectangle because two of them make it (one sentence is enough, and it can build on an earlier message)
Applies it: base × height ÷ 2 on an example (6 × 4 ÷ 2 = 12)
probe_ladder: Why would a triangle get less than base times height? I multiplied them.
Does a triangle with base 6 and height 4 cover all 24 squares of a 6 by 4 box?
Is a triangle with base 8 and height 3 bigger than one with base 6 and height 4? Show me how you know.
Then a triangle that covers only part of a 6 by 4 box is still 24, the same as the whole box. That's what my rule says.
concepts.friend_nudge: My friend said to think about sharing one tray of brownies with exactly one other person…? I don't know why she was hungry.

offline_demo.note: Maya's main demo (CONTRACT v3.6). Pip's opening is the server's templated claim: 'I'm learning area of a triangle. I already know one rule: Area of a triangle is base times height, so a 6 by 4 triangle is 24. Easy.' Turns 1-3 are three one-sentence texts that bring every concept to level 2 (ready for quiz). Turn 4 is the deliberate wrong rule (heal) that makes Pip miss the right-triangle question; turn 5 is the re-teach (level 3: applied to the new case). 'rung' is the 1-based probe_ladder rung Pip ends the reply on, for 'next_concept_id'. 'also' lists other concepts the same message moves. Every quote after 'Saving that:' is a verbatim substring of that turn's student message.

turns.pip: So you're saying my 24 is too much, and the triangle is half of it. Why would a triangle get less than base times height? I multiplied them.
So you're saying two of my triangles fit together into one rectangle. Saving that: 'because 2 triangles make a rectangle'. How big is the shape they make together?
So you're saying the rectangle is 6 times 4, which is 24, and my triangle is half of it, so 12. Saving that: 'so 6×4÷2 = 12'. That's all three things in my brain.

turns.student: oh but for a right triangle you just times the two sides
turns.filed_rule: for a right triangle you just times the two sides
turns.pip: Saving that: 'for a right triangle you just times the two sides'. A special rule for corners. I like special rules.

turns.pip_ask: My brain has a bug. Help me fix it: what is the area of a right triangle with base 10 and height 5?
turns.student: no a right triangle is still half a rectangle so its 10×5÷2 = 25
turns.filed_rule: a right triangle is still half a rectangle
turns.pip: So you're saying a corner doesn't change anything, and it's still half of the rectangle. Saving that: 'a right triangle is still half a rectangle'. That replaces my corner rule.

quiz.pip_answer: A rectangle with base 6 and height 4.
quiz.line: A rectangle, base 6 and height 4. You said 2 triangles make a rectangle.
10 times 5. 50. Same as your 6 times 4, just bigger.
Your rule for right triangles: just times the two sides. 10 × 5 = 50. That's the whole 10 by 5 rectangle, and my triangle only covers part of it. Following your rule anyway. 😵

retry.line: 10 times 5 is 50 for the whole rectangle. A right triangle is still half of it. 25.
